subject: Accounting
title: Keep or Drop a Product Line
description: Learn Keep or Drop a Product Line in one minute.

hook.text: The bakery's muffin line loses $2,000 a month. Should you drop it? Not so fast.

buildup.text: Dropping a product eliminates its revenue and variable costs—but fixed costs often remain.

discovery.text: If the muffin line covers its variable costs and part of the fixed costs, dropping it could make things worse.

twist.text: Customers who come for muffins also buy coffee and pastries. Losing them could shrink total sales.

climax.text: The decision requires analyzing contribution margin, avoidable costs, and customer behavior.

punchline.text: A losing product might still be carrying its weight.

quiz.question: Why might a company keep a money-losing product line?
options: It may still cover variable costs and some fixed costs

details.summary: The keep-or-drop decision evaluates whether a product line, segment, or department should continue operating or be eliminated. This topic explains how to analyze relevant costs and revenues, identify avoidable vs. unavoidable costs, and avoid common analytical traps.
details.whyItMatters: A product line showing a loss on paper may actually contribute to covering fixed costs. Dropping it without proper analysis can make overall profits worse, not better.
takeaways: Only avoidable costs—those that disappear if the line is dropped—are relevant to the decision
Allocated fixed costs that continue regardless should be excluded from the analysis
A product line with a positive contribution margin usually should be kept even if it shows an accounting loss

faq.question: How do you decide whether to keep or drop a product line?
faq.answer: Compare the revenue lost from dropping the line against the costs that would actually be avoided. If the line's revenue exceeds its avoidable costs (those that disappear with it), keeping it is better—even if allocated fixed costs make it look unprofitable on paper.

faq.question: Why might a company keep a product line that appears unprofitable?
faq.answer: Because allocated common fixed costs can make a line appear to lose money when it actually generates a positive contribution margin. If those fixed costs continue regardless, dropping the line eliminates revenue without eliminating the costs, worsening overall profit.
